book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch

chapters.file: ch20 - Become a Work of Art!.md
chapters.relation: Dumitrica reads iPod customization (skins, colors, playlists) as a Foucauldian technology of the self: identity is not a stable inner core but something continually made, as when a Facebook user who loses her 80G black iPod feels 'empty'. Against Foucault's examples of ancient care of the self and Christian confessional self-renunciation, she argues the iPod embodies the modern disciplinary self: we survey our playlists against what friends will think, dividing practices split iPod owners from users of 'lame MP3 or CD-players', and social-science-style lifestyle classifications (hip-hop vs heavy metal) shape our choices. The chapter ends by urging Foucault's aesthetic escape from pre-packaged lifestyle models — treat the self as a work of art, like the author sharing holiday photos with her father instead of plunging into a self-enclosed sonic bubble.

Turner runs an ethical audit of iPod use through Levinas's face-to-face: sharing one iPod with his wife forces 'musical justice' negotiations (veto power over a Motörhead cut, gnashing through Bette Midler), his toddler son's listening requires vigilance, and illegal downloading fails Levinas's test that morality begins by ceding 'my place in the sun' to the Other — hence Radiohead's pay-what-you-want release as the Levinasian move, and iPod cafés where strangers DJ for each other while language preserves alterity. Heidegger supplies the counterweight: the shuffle's 'openness to mystery' versus calculative mastery that reduces The Who's Tommy to the 'Pinball Wizard' riff and silences all non-digital media, just as Kant's conditions of possible experience (space, time) would silence things outside them. Derrida's point that categories contain traces of what they exclude illuminates unclassifiable marginal works — bluegrass Pink Floyd, San Francisco Symphony plays Metallica — and the verdict closes with Hölderlin's 'where danger is, grows the saving power also', exiting Plato's cave by thinking the iPod's ethics at all.

Pitt argues the iPod is 'pernicious' not because technology is intrinsically bad — a device is judged by the uses it is put to and their consequences — but because its consequences are antisocial: silent subways, 'brainsnatched' beach-walkers, and the silenced graduate corridor where loud philosophical argument used to live. Comparing the gadget to Huxley's soma (each user programs his own blissful isolation, going so far as to avoid domestic conflict by plugging back in), he contends social skills — argument, eye contact, advocacy for ideas — are what drive both technological innovation (even Steve Jobs had a co-inventor) and functioning democracy. Hence the earbud habituation summarized as 'Don't talk to me, I'm listening to MY music!' is, he claims, one of the final nails in the coffin of the social skills a civil, democratic society needs.

Kaulingfreks and Warren answer the charge that iPods destroy community with Jean-Luc Nancy: the warm organic community the iPod allegedly replaced is a romantic myth, because being is always 'singular plural' — we are only individuals in relation to others, and politicizing community into organized identity leads to totalitarianism. Gadamer's claim that art creates its own community (the tennis crowd's swaying necks, the party's ekstasis) explains how white earbuds already signal a shared passion even in solitude, while Nietzsche (art gives the distance needed to comprehend the world) and Heidegger (art transports us into the work's own space and time) justify the retreat into music as anything but antisocial. Their exhibit is 'mobile clubbing' — thousands converging on London stations and the Tate to dance to their own iPods, together yet each on a different beat — an inoperative community, together without forming a club, whose only bond is the recognition of being-with.

Dewey takes the iPod's beauty seriously (Chris Breen's 'beautiful and intuitive' player, Donald Norman's user-centered design) and uses John Dewey's Art as Experience to ask whether iPod use can be a 'consummatory' experience that ends with us no longer the same person — hearing a bitter song as insight into the social conditions that produced it — rather than the contrived 'now' of fashion and hyper-accumulation, per Benjamin's remark that there is 'always a sense of the same in the new'. Mass production flattened the aristocratic high-culture/folk division and handed the power to define 'cool' to advertisers and the market. The pragmatist test is political: with iTunes DRM and single-user design quietly individualizing consumption (the ritual of buying the Public Enemy tape at the mall versus the frictionless one-click download), the iPod is beautiful exactly insofar as its experiences help form a public — an inclusive, participatory democratic community.

This edited LibriVox podcast transcript catches three volunteers debating free culture: Wittkower argues copyright is an artificial monopoly justified only when printing presses made reproducing texts capital-intensive — now that consumer gear has put industrial-scale production in everyone's basement ('the working man has wrested the means of production from the big man'), a thirteen-year-old should be free to strip vocals and remix her culture. McGaughey's title thesis — cheap technology means a quantitative change becomes a qualitative change, 'which is by the way from Hegel's Logic' — answers Mowatt's deflation that the Internet merely lowers the bar for things you could always have done locally. Connecting Putnam's Bowling Alone decline of social trust to narrow-casting as a way of rebuilding communities of common concern, they hold up LibriVox's 1,668 free public-domain audiobooks (327 days of audio, volunteers on six continents) as a gift-economy counter-model to a culture we only 'rent' as serfs on branded soil.

Arnold coins 'podcrastination' — the voluntary suspension of engagement with reality — and tests podcasting against two poles: Adorno's consciousness industry, under which plugging into an administered device is a 'cyborgian opiate' that deepens our thrall (CBS's listener-programmed KYOU station is still 'administrated'), and Postman's warning that 'we are tools of our tools'. The chapter's spine is Enzensberger's 1970 socialist media theory: podcasting fulfills his eight emancipatory criteria — decentralized programming, each receiver a potential transmitter, interaction, feedback, mobilization, political learning, self-organization — and could coordinate 'smart mobs' like the text-messaging crowds that toppled Estrada at Manila's EDSA plaza. Yet the media's potential is betrayed as much as realized — the Abu Ghraib photos and the 'Macaca' video circulated without catalyzing change — so the prediction is that the podcast will be squandered rather than co-opted: the iPod 'is not going to further a cyborg manifesto. It's only going to create a cyborg lament.'

Lombardo asks whether the podcast, born as an unsanctioned side effect users reinvented out of the iPod (as hip hop reinvented the turntable before corporate co-option made it the hegemonic form), can be a public-sphere institution. Following Habermas's Structural Transformation — coffeehouses, salons, and a subscription-financed press later corrupted by advertising into 'the soft compulsion of constant consumption-training' — and Dewey's call in The Public and Its Problems for institutions people actually participate in, he argues podcasts resemble the liberal-era press: resistant to advertising (readily fast-forwarded or deleted), enthusiast- and subscriber-funded, and open to marginal voices like a 'gun-owning, gay Texan' commentator that gatekept mass media would never air. But most Web 2.0 talk merely supplements advertising with consumerist pseudo-debate, so podcasts must link their fragmented diversity into a broader conversation of public relevance to become a socially transformative public sphere rather than 150,000 isolated niches.

A comic Socratic dialogue, a pastiche of Plato's Phaedrus, in which a time-lost 'Rhodesian Stranger' wanders in mid-conversation to defend reading against Socrates' retelling of the Thamus-and-Thoth myth — writing as inert painting that gives 'the semblance of truth', summed up in the Stranger's quoting his 'fellow Rhodish' philosopher Schopenhauer: thoughts on paper are footprints in the sand, the path seen but not what was seen along the way. Socrates' elenchus (the ship ticket versus the journey, walking beside a friend and turning back to check on him rather than posting signposts) drives the Stranger into inventing a myth in which gods replace abused speech with pea-pods whose planted seeds become pod-casts gathered by pod-catchers — podcasting imagined as friends dialoguing together toward the true and the good. Socrates closes skeptically, doubting that disconnected pod-communication escapes trivia and universal broadcast, but concedes 'surely beauty is as faithful a guide towards the good as is truth.'

holes.name: Jean-Luc Nancy
holes.what: French philosopher whose The Inoperative Community argues community is never a lost organic whole nor a common identity, but an always-given 'being-with' in singular plurality that resists organization and politicization.
holes.why: Chapter 24's central claim — that iPod mobile clubbing is a genuine community without shared identity, and that the 'lost community' is a myth — is Nancy's doctrine outright, and no taxonomy slug covers it.

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: German hermeneutic philosopher whose Truth and Method and The Relevance of the Beautiful treat the artwork as play that draws spectators into its own realm and thereby gathers a community (the festival, the tennis crowd).
holes.why: Chapter 24 uses Gadamer's account of art creating its own community and leaving each participant a personal space as the bridge between iPod solitude and togetherness, and no taxonomy slug covers him.

holes.name: Technologies of the Self (care of the self)
holes.what: Foucault's late-work concept for the practices (diet, writing, confession, meditation) through which individuals effect operations on their own bodies and souls so as to transform themselves toward happiness, purity, or wisdom.
holes.why: Chapter 20 applies technologies of the self directly to the iPod — playlist-making and customization as self-formation, from ancient self-care to Christian confession to modern preference-lists — which the power-focused Foucault slugs do not capture.

holes.name: Hans Magnus Enzensberger
holes.what: German essayist and media theorist whose 'Constituents of a Theory of the Media' (1970) lists the emancipatory potentials of new media: decentralized programming, each receiver a potential transmitter, mobilization, interaction, feedback, political learning, collective production, and self-organization.
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire framework evaluates podcasting point-by-point against Enzensberger's eight criteria for an emancipatory socialist media, and no taxonomy philosopher or slug covers this media-emancipation theory.
